sections.content: Jeanne Dielman (1975) revolutionized cinema by turning mundane domestic routines into a masterpiece of slow-burning tension. Director Chantal Akerman's groundbreaking 3.5-hour film follows three days in the life of a widowed housewife, using fixed camera positions and real-time sequences to document her methodical daily tasks. The film's influence echoes through works like Safe (1995) and The Hours (2002), which similarly examine women's domestic imprisonment. Akerman's radical approach - showing nearly every minute of Jeanne's cooking, cleaning, and sex work - transformed how cinema could depict female experience and everyday life.

sections.content: The film's revolutionary treatment of time and space created a new language for feminist cinema. While Hollywood relegated domestic work to quick montages, Akerman forced viewers to experience every moment of Jeanne's confined existence. This influenced later works like Wendy and Lucy (2008) and 45 Years (2015), which similarly use duration and quiet observation to explore female isolation. The film's clinical framing and attention to gesture anticipates Michael Haneke's style in films like The Piano Teacher (2001) and Amour (2012).

Akerman's masterpiece sparked a wave of feminist experimental films that challenged traditional narrative structures. News from Home (1977) continued her exploration of alienation through static shots of New York paired with letters from her mother. The influence extends to contemporary filmmakers like Kelly Reichardt, whose Meek's Cutoff (2010) and Certain Women (2016) share Jeanne Dielman's patient observation of women's work and inner lives. sections.content: Modern filmmakers continue drawing from Akerman's revolutionary approach. Phantom Thread (2017) echoes Jeanne Dielman's attention to domestic ritual and power dynamics, while The Assistant (2019) adopts its clinical observation of workplace routines. The film's influence extends beyond art house cinema - even mainstream works like Carol (2015) and Portrait of a Lady on Fire (2019) inherit its careful attention to female desire and domestic space.
